text.p: Bosnia's collective presidency on Thursday agreed to nominate a Moslem and a Serb to chair a peacetime central government in what mediators called a "step forward" for the peace process.

The former prime minister of Bosnia, Haris Silajdzic, was chosen as the Moslem representative and Boro Bosic, a Serb and former manager of a power plant was selected as the other chairman of the council of ministers, the presidency said in a statement.
The two men will act as joint prime ministers of a weak central government overseeing three ministries for foreign affairs, foreign trade and civil affairs and communications.

The international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, and other diplomats welcomed the announcement after Moslem, Serb and Croat leaders spent weeks haggling over the structure of the new government.
"I congratulate the members of the presidency on reaching this important agreement. This is an important step forward for Bosnia," Bildt said in a statement.
The peace agreement preserved Bosnia as a loose union comprised of a Serb republic and a Moslem-Croat federation.
Appointments for ministers and deputy ministers are to be distributed among Bosnia's Moslem, Serb and Croat communities.
The nomination gave a boost to Silajdzic's political career after his own party's poor showing in post-war elections.

Silajdzic broke with the main Moslem party, the Party of Democratic Action (SDA), during the war and resigned as prime minister in January, accusing the SDA of pursuing nationalist aims and forsaking democratic principles.
He formed his own party and ran as a candidate for the presidency in the country's first peacetime elections held in September.
Silajdzic lost to Alija Izetbegovic, wartime president and SDA leader, who was elected as the chairman of the new three-man collective presidency.
Silajdzic became a familiar figure in the Western media during the Bosnian conflict, appealing for military intervention to end the Serb siege of Sarajevo.
In November 1995, he played a central role at peace talks in the United States that led to the signing of a peace treaty ending four years of war in former Yugoslavia.
Bosic is a former manager of a power plant in Ugljevik in northeast Bosnia and former energy minister in Bosnia's Serb republic.
The nominations still have to be formally approved by the national parliament, the House of Representatives, later this month.
